title: ASME Stamp Audit NDE Support in Los Angeles, CA
description: LA basin vessel, exchanger and repair shops: Level III prep of the NDE side of an ASME or R review for Cal/OSHA, LADBS and owner specs. Request a gap review.
h1: ASME Certification Audit Support in Los Angeles: NDE Readiness Under State, City and Refinery Rules
html:
Pressure-equipment shops in the Los Angeles basin answer to more parties than most: ASME and their Authorized Inspection Agency, California's Pressure Vessel Unit, the City of Los Angeles for equipment inside city limits, and refinery or oilfield owners with specifications of their own. Atlantis NDT is a consulting firm built around ASNT NDT Level III expertise, and before a certificate review, initial or renewal, ASME or National Board R, we get your NDE controls into a state that every one of those readers will accept. Write to us about your certificate scope; we reply within one business day.

What gets built and repaired around Los Angeles

The basin's pressure-equipment market is shaped by a handful of industries that sit close together. Refineries in the South Bay and harbor area run large inventories of vessels, exchangers and piping and buy repair work at every turnaround. Oil production continues inside the urban footprint, with fields producing through separators, heater-treaters and gathering lines that need vessels and periodic repair. The twin ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach bring terminals, bulk-liquid storage and the compressed-air systems of a huge logistics operation. Aerospace and defense manufacturers run test stands, autoclaves and high-pressure gas systems. Add commercial boilers in high-rise buildings, industrial gas distribution and food processing, and the region keeps a wide range of Code shops busy.

Those shops tend to be specialized rather than general. Some build Section VIII Division 1 receivers, separators and filter housings in volume. Some focus on heat exchanger repair and re-tubing under an R certificate for the refineries. Some build high-pressure vessels and gas-system components where Division 2 or heavy-wall work comes into play. Others are field organizations that make repairs inside plant fences. The common thread is that California requires permits on a large population of equipment, so the paperwork a shop produces is read by state or city inspectors for the life of each vessel.

California's Pressure Vessel Unit

Statewide, boilers and pressure vessels are regulated by the Pressure Vessel Unit of Cal/OSHA, part of the Department of Industrial Relations, under Labor Code sections 7620 through 7771 and two sets of Title 8 safety orders: the Unfired Pressure Vessel Safety Orders (sections 450 to 560) and the Boiler and Fired Pressure Vessel Safety Orders (sections 750 to 797). The unit's southern office in Santa Ana covers Los Angeles County and the rest of Southern California. Points that bear on a Code shop:

  • Permits to Operate on a wide range of equipment. Air tanks above a small volume, LP-gas tanks above a modest capacity and power boilers above 15 psig need a Permit to Operate. Inspections for a permit are made by a Pressure Vessel Unit inspector or by a qualified inspector employed by an insurance company.
  • ASME construction and registration. The National Board's synopsis of state laws shows California requiring ASME construction and National Board registration for pressure vessels, with UM vessels the stated exception, and listing a recent ASME Code edition along with recent B31.1, B31.3 and B31.5 editions. Non-ASME or foreign designs need the Division's acceptance.
  • Repairs and alterations. The same synopsis records that no alteration or repair is made without the authorization of a qualified inspector, and it lists the NBIC with a different edition for refineries than for other locations. Its note on R-stamp requirements treats refinery and oilfield locations differently from others, so confirm with the unit what a given repair site requires before you plan the job.
  • Owner-user programs. Owner-user organizations with in-service programs approved by the unit can employ qualified inspectors who authorize repairs and alterations, which is common at large refineries.

The Pressure Vessel Unit also publishes circular letters on Code topics, from steam boiler ASME requirements to exchanger design rules. A quality manager should read the current ones before a review; they show which issues the state inspectors who read your data reports care about.

The City of Los Angeles runs its own program

Inside city limits, permits for boilers and pressure vessels come from the Los Angeles Department of Building and Safety rather than the state. The National Board lists the City of Los Angeles as a separate member jurisdiction, and its synopsis entry describes a Pressure Vessel Section that commissions owner-user inspectors, requires an annual external inspection on covered equipment and inspects air tanks every three years. The same entry lists consultation, surveys, audits and manual reviews among the section's chargeable services, so a shop located within the city may find the city involved at review time. The entry's listed Code edition is old and may not reflect current practice; check the edition in force directly with the department's pressure vessel desk.

The practical consequence is that a vessel built in a Commerce or Vernon shop, installed at a refinery in Wilmington and repaired later by a field crew can pass through two jurisdictions and several inspectors. Each of them reads the NDE record on the data report or R form, so that record needs to be complete and traceable the first time.

Refinery work and California's process safety rules

California holds its refineries to a dedicated process safety management standard in Title 8, separate from and more detailed than the federal rule. For the fabricators and repair firms that serve those refineries, the effect shows up in owner specifications and supplier audits rather than in the ASME Code itself. Typical requirements flowed down from South Bay owners include:

  • Radiography or ultrasonic examination of every inch of seams where Division 1 would accept spot examination, with UT permitted in place of RT only under a procedure the owner has accepted.
  • Owner review and acceptance of NDE procedures and of the examiners who will perform them.
  • Positive material identification and hardness testing alongside the NDE, especially on alloy and sour-service equipment.
  • Specific report formats, weld maps and a turnover package that matches the owner's mechanical integrity records.

Your QC manual should explain how purchaser requirements like these are captured at contract review, turned into an examination plan, performed to an identified procedure, and recorded so that both the Code and the specification are visibly satisfied. A review team that finds added examinations in a job file with no procedure behind them will ask what controlled the work. Our El Segundo refining NDT consulting and Torrance refining NDT consulting pages cover Level III work at the refinery level.

Radiography in California and the subcontractor file

California is an Agreement State, so industrial radiography companies here are licensed by the state's radiologic health program rather than directly by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, and their radiographers carry state certification. Most Los Angeles Code shops buy radiography rather than holding a license themselves. Atlantis is not a radiography company and makes no exposures in the United States. Our Level III contribution is on paper and film: reviewing images and technique details, checking reports against the procedure, and drafting the radiographic requirements your shop sets for its lab.

For the review, the radiography subcontractor's file in your office should hold its license, the written practice it certifies people under, up-to-date credentials for whoever exposes and reads your film, its procedure with your acceptance recorded, and the radiographs or digital images for your Code jobs. ASME's joint review guidance expects the procedure and personnel qualifications of subcontracted NDE to be available where the review takes place. The same file discipline applies to the ultrasonic, magnetic particle and penetrant companies you use; the method on our subcontractor approval audits page shows how we build it.

How the review team will test your NDE controls

The joint review runs in two stages. First the team examines your quality control manual. Then it comes to your facility and watches the manual in operation on Code work in progress, on a mock-up made for the purpose, or both, and the demonstration has to suit each designator you request. In a Los Angeles receiver or separator shop, a good demonstration item has a longitudinal seam with spot or full radiography, nozzle welds with magnetic particle examination, and a hydrostatic test. A Division 2 applicant needs a design package suited to that division as well.

On the NDE side, the team checks that your written practice covers every method you perform in the right SNT-TC-1A or CP-189 edition; that procedures meet Section V (Article 1 for general requirements, Article 2 for radiography, Article 4 for weld ultrasonics, Article 7 for magnetic particle); that someone in your company reviewed outside reports before the Authorized Inspector did; and that every instrument used on Code work was in calibration. On a renewal, the NDE records behind any job on your Code work list are open to sampling.

NDE findings we often see in basin shops:

  • Owner-added UT performed to a procedure the QC manual never mentions.
  • A radiography lab whose state license copy in the shop file had expired.
  • Examiners from an outside company who were never formally accepted before working on Code welds.
  • Magnetic particle yokes with lift tests done but not recorded, and black lights with no intensity checks on file.
  • Repair packages for refinery work missing the record of which inspector authorized the repair.
  • Data reports summarizing NDE that the job file cannot fully support.

Atlantis's support for Los Angeles shops

Los Angeles work is run from Atlantis's Houston office. Document review, drafting and gap reports are done remotely, and we fly in for the site portion. A typical engagement includes:

  • A line-by-line comparison of your manual's NDE chapters with the Code edition your jurisdiction applies, the Title 8 safety orders where they touch construction and repair, and your main customers' specifications.
  • Revision of the written practice, including owner-accepted examiners and the rules for outside personnel.
  • Section V procedures and technique sheets through our procedure development service, including UT procedures written for owner requirements to replace radiography.
  • Preparation for a procedure demonstration where your Authorized Inspector or the owner asks to witness one.
  • A check of every examiner file you will show the team, plus Level III examinations administered the way your written practice describes; the certification signature remains your employer's.
  • A mock implementation at your shop, then help closing any findings with corrective-action evidence.

Engagements are led by Atlantis's founder, Anoop Rayavarapu, whose ASNT NDT Level III covers radiographic, ultrasonic, magnetic particle, penetrant and visual testing, and he has worked in the field for more than 11 years on projects inside and outside the United States. Level III work beyond audits is described on our Los Angeles NDT consulting page; for examiner training, see NDT training in Los Angeles; and for in-service examinations, see pressure vessel inspection in Los Angeles.

The boundaries of our role

Atlantis advises and prepares; it does not judge. The ASME team, your Authorized Inspection Agency and any state or city representative evaluate your system, and ASME issues or renews the certificate. Atlantis holds no inspection commission, signs no data report or R form, and is not a certification body. Your company owns its manual, makes every change to it, and certifies its own NDE personnel.

Welding procedures and welder qualification under Section IX are your welding engineer's responsibility; Atlantis does not write WPS or PQR documents or qualify procedures, and the WPS, PQR and WPQ article explains that program. Nuclear work is outside our scope: we support no Section III construction, no N-type certificates and no NQA-1 programs.

Los Angeles readiness checklist

  • You know whether the State Pressure Vessel Unit or the City of Los Angeles is your jurisdiction for the review, and which edition each applies.
  • The current Pressure Vessel Unit circular letters relevant to your scope have been read and, where needed, reflected in your manual.
  • Contract review captures owner NDE requirements and the manual names the procedure for each added examination.
  • Your radiography subcontractor's California license, written practice, radiographer certifications and accepted procedure are on file and current.
  • Every outside NDE company has an acceptance file in your office, and outside examiners are accepted before they work on Code welds.
  • Written practice, manual and procedures name a single SNT-TC-1A or CP-189 edition consistent with your Code edition.
  • Yokes, flaw detectors, gauges, light meters and reference blocks are on one calibration register with nothing overdue in use.
  • Repair packages record which qualified inspector authorized each repair or alteration and show NDE to the original code of construction.
  • Data reports and R forms can be backed line by line by the job file's NDE records.
  • The piece you will demonstrate on calls for each NDE method you hold yourself out as controlling, and its records run unbroken from traveler to data report.

What to send us and how the work runs

To start, send the NDE sections of your quality control manual, the written practice, your procedure index, three examiner certification files, the subcontractor files for each NDE company, your calibration register and one completed job package, preferably one that carried owner-added examinations. For a renewal, include your draft Code work list. After a scoping call we return a written gap report keyed to the Code and practice clauses, draft corrections for your quality manager to approve, schedule the site visit for a mock implementation and records walkthrough, and remain on call through the review and the close-out of any findings. For the wider picture, read our nationwide guide to ASME audit Level III support; repair organizations should also see NDE support for National Board R-stamp reviews. Our NDT audit consulting page describes the general audit method.

faq.q: Is our jurisdiction the State of California or the City of Los Angeles?
faq.a: Equipment installed inside Los Angeles city limits is permitted through the city's Department of Building and Safety; elsewhere in the state the Cal/OSHA Pressure Vessel Unit applies. For the review itself, ask your Authorized Inspection Agency which jurisdiction will participate, especially if your shop sits inside the city.

faq.q: Do California pressure vessels need National Board registration?
faq.a: The National Board's synopsis shows California requiring National Board registration for pressure vessels, with UM vessels as the stated exception. Confirm current requirements with the Pressure Vessel Unit before relying on that for a specific job.

faq.q: Who authorizes a repair at a refinery in California?
faq.a: California requires repairs and alterations to be authorized by a qualified inspector, and large refineries often run approved owner-user programs with their own qualified inspectors. Record that authorization in the repair package, because review teams and state inspectors both look for it.

faq.q: Our refinery customer wants UT instead of RT. What must our manual cover?
faq.a: A UT procedure that meets the applicable Section V and construction-code conditions, examiners qualified for it, owner acceptance where the specification calls for it, and a contract-review step that shows how the requirement reached the shop floor. See our procedure development page.

faq.q: What belongs in our radiography subcontractor file?
faq.a: Its state radiography license, the written practice behind its personnel, credentials for the people who shoot and interpret your work, its procedure with your acceptance noted, evidence of equipment calibration, and the images for your Code jobs. Keep the whole file at your facility for the review.

faq.q: Can Atlantis perform radiography for our shop?
faq.a: No. Atlantis is not licensed for industrial radiography in the United States and makes no exposures here. We review radiographs, techniques and reports as a Level III.

faq.q: Can Atlantis act as our outside agency Level III?
faq.a: Yes, where your written practice allows it, for ultrasonic, radiographic, magnetic particle, penetrant and visual testing. Your company still certifies its own examiners. See Level III consulting.

faq.q: Do the Title 8 safety orders change how we do NDE on new vessels?
faq.a: New construction follows the ASME Code your jurisdiction adopts. The safety orders matter most for permits, inspections, repairs and alterations, and the Pressure Vessel Unit's circular letters show where state inspectors focus. Read both before finalizing your manual revision.

faq.q: Will Atlantis prepare our WPS and PQR files for the review?
faq.a: No. Those files are part of the welding program your welding engineer owns, and drafting or qualifying them is not a service Atlantis provides.

faq.q: How is a Los Angeles engagement split between remote and on-site work?
faq.a: Everything that is paper, from reading the manual to drafting fixes, happens remotely. The trip to Los Angeles is for rehearsing implementation on the shop floor and going through files with your staff, plus any examinations that are better given face to face.
